structure.title: Returning to Abraham
structure.text: Opening retellings make a familiar biblical journey strange again. Praise and imagined variations prepare the philosophical difficulty.

structure.title: Three problems
structure.text: The central investigations consider ethics, duty to God, and Abraham's silence. Each revisits the limits of explaining his act publicly.

people.name: Abraham
people.text: The patriarch whom God commands to sacrifice his son Isaac, and whose willingness to obey Kierkegaard finds both admirable and terrifying.

people.name: Johannes de silentio
people.text: The pseudonym Kierkegaard writes under, a man who says he admires Abraham's faith and cannot understand it.

people.name: The ethical
people.text: The moral law that applies to everyone; the book asks whether faith could ever require someone to step outside it.

context.title: Genesis 22
context.text: Read Genesis 22:1–19 before you start: God tells Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac on a mountain in Moriah; Abraham goes, binds him and raises the knife, and an angel stops him. The pseudonymous author retells the story four ways at the outset and asks what Abraham's faith can mean.
context.takeaway: Keep the father and son in view.

context.title: A pseudonymous voice
context.text: The speaker repeatedly describes limits to his own understanding of faith. His position should not be flattened into a direct authorial instruction.

notice.text: Compare Abraham with publicly intelligible heroes.
notice.why: Their sacrifices can be explained in terms his cannot easily share.
Silence affects the possibility of justification.

opening: Abraham takes his son up a mountain intending to obey God's command to sacrifice him. The story is familiar enough to be told reverently without much alarm. Kierkegaard restores the alarm. From outside Abraham's faith, his intention looks monstrous; from inside it, he is supposed to be exemplary. The book keeps returning to the journey and the silence between father and son, refusing to let religious admiration become an easy way of avoiding what the person being admired was prepared to do.
